body: `order()` is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any third-party or downstream `CryptoProvider` implementation, including the copy that will be synced to keycloak-client, stops compiling. Already-compiled implementations throw `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the sort comparator. Make it a `default` method (e.g. `return 0;`) to keep backward compatibility.

This drops the old 'multiple crypto providers' safety check. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so when two of them are on the classpath (e.g. default + fips1402 by mistake) the choice depends on ServiceLoader/classpath order, and the only trace is a debug log. That can silently run a FIPS deployment on the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider. At minimum, keep failing (or warn) when the top two providers have the same order; the ignored-providers message should also be logged at WARN/INFO rather than debug.

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (typically `SUN`), not BouncyCastle. `CryptoIntegration.init` touches `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER`, so this fixes `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` to e.g. "SUN" for the whole JVM. Code that later does `Signature/Cipher/KeyFactory.getInstance(..., BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` then quietly uses a JDK provider under a misleading name. Returning `null` makes `BouncyIntegration` fall back explicitly, which would be clearer and safer.

Inconsistent with the other providers: they use `format.toString()` together with a specific provider. With the plain JDK, `KeystoreFormat.BCFKS` throws `KeyStoreException` here, so using a BCFKS truststore/keystore through the authz client will fail at runtime. At least document this or map it to a clear error.
Dead code: these two encoders are created and discarded because the real encoding happens again below. Remove them.

`integerToBytes` silently drops the high-order bytes when r/s is longer than `qLength` (beyond the single 0x00 sign byte). A malformed or oversized DER integer gets converted into a different, truncated value instead of being rejected. Only allow dropping a leading zero byte; otherwise throw `IOException`. Negative r/s (sign bit set with no leading zero) should also be rejected.

`readLength()` returns -1 for indefinite length. `readSequence` then returns an empty list, but in `readNext()`/`readInteger()` the -1 reaches `read(length)` → `new byte[-1]` → `NegativeArraySizeException`, a RuntimeException instead of an `IOException`. DER forbids indefinite length, so throw `IOException` here. Also, short-form lengths skip the bounds check that long-form lengths get.

A zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) makes `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throw `NumberFormatException`, which is not the `IOException` callers expect. Also, `readSequence()` never checks that the sequence length matches the buffer, so trailing garbage after the SEQUENCE is silently accepted. Validate both cases.

The key pair is generated with the default EC size (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512. Those tests therefore never produce real P-384/P-521 signatures: r/s are always at most 32 bytes and just get zero-padded, so the 66-byte ES512 case with a leading sign byte is never exercised. Generate a key on the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1). Also consider verifying the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, not just round-tripping.
